transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-30
Start Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Liam Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Mark Dawson (Altair HoCS), Elena Ruiz (Altair VP Eng), Ravi Patel (Infra Lead), Sophie Tran (Compliance)

Summary: deep dive into Private/VPC deployment model, network isolation, ingress/egress controls, firewalling, KMS/HSM integration, SOC 2/ISO artifacts, RBAC/SSO and audit logging to SIEM. Customer shared constraints around strict egress controls, data residency in eu-west-1 and us-east-1, and preference for HSM-backed keys on-prem for certain PI data.

Topics: private VPC architecture, transit gateway vs peering, ingress patterns (bastion, private endpoints, ALB), egress proxy & NAT, firewall rule template, security group design, KMS/HSM integration, key rotation, audit log forwarding, SAML/SCIM provisioning, RBAC scopes, SOC 2 evidence, pen test and config management.

[00:00] Liam: Hey everyone thanks for joining, um I'm Liam from Redwood, I'll kick off — Priya will run the deep technical bits. Can everyone see the agenda I shared?
[00:12] Mark: Yep we can see it. Thanks. Quick context: Altair runs a hybrid cloud, most services in AWS but some legacy on-prem. We have strict egress policy, everything must go through the egress proxy and approved destinations only.
[00:26] Priya: Got it. We'll focus on how Redwood Private can sit in your VPCs with no public ingress, controllable egress, and KMS/HSM options. First question — do you plan to host model artifacts in your VPC or use Redwood's S3-backed artifact store?
[00:40] Elena: For regulated workloads we want artifacts in our control, so ideally host model artifacts in our S3 behind VPC endpoints, and for some high-risk models keep them on-prem.
[00:53] Priya: Makes sense. So two patterns: 1) fully private in your AWS account with VPC endpoints for S3, NAT/egress through your proxy and private endpoints for control-plane; 2) on-prem variant where the runtime runs in a customer datacenter and talks to a private control plane or offline artifact sync. We'll dig into network diagrams in a bit.
[01:12] Ravi: Quick question — if we do the AWS VPC option, what's the connectivity model? Do we need VPC peering or a transit gateway?
[01:20] Priya: Good question. For small setups peering can work, but at scale we recommend Transit Gateway (TGW) for centralized routing, especially across multiple AZs and accounts. Redwood supports either; we provide recommended route tables and security-group templates.
[01:39] Mark: We run multiple accounts across regions, TGW is our standard. Concern is route propagation and ensuring no accidental default routes to the internet.
[01:48] Priya: Absolutely — we recommend explicit route tables, no 0.0.0.0/0 to IGW in subnets, and enforce egress via a dedicated egress VPC with NATs and egress proxy. Redwood's Private nodes can be placed in isolated private subnets with no IGW, and we only allow outbound to the egress proxy IPs or to your approved S3 endpoints.
[02:10] Liam: Also quick note, for customers that require zero internet egress, we support an air-gapped mode where artifact sync is manual or via a controlled jump host.
[02:21] Sophie: On KMS, our compliance team requires HSM-backed keys for certain datasets; AWS KMS with imported key material isn't acceptable for those. Can Redwood integrate with an on-prem HSM or external KMS?
[02:32] Priya: Yes. We support multiple key management patterns: 1) customer-managed cloud KMS (AWS KMS / GCP KMS) with BYOK, 2) external HSM via PKCS#11 for on-prem or HSM appliances, and 3) Redwood-managed encryption for lower-risk workloads. For HSM, the runtime is configured to call the HSM over a secure channel inside your network — we don't store private key material in Redwood's control plane.
[02:54] Mark: That sounds good. Do you have examples for key rotation and auditability?
[02:59] Priya: We log key usage to the audit trail (detailed logs of unwrap/wrap operations), and recommend rotation windows (90 days for high-risk keys is common). We can show an example terraform and rotation policy.
[03:12] Elena: Regarding audit logs — we forward application, audit and runtime logs to customer SIEM, correct? We don't want logs stored in Redwood beyond X days.
[03:21] Liam: Correct, we can push logs to your CloudWatch, GCS, or to an on-prem SIEM via syslog/HTTPS. We also offer retention controls and can disable storage in Redwood for PII-sensitive payloads.
[03:34] Sophie: Are request/response payloads ever stored in plaintext in logs? That's our main worry.
[03:40] Priya: We have redaction options at ingestion. By default, we persist minimal metadata for operational reasons; payloads are not stored unless you enable request logging. For SOC 2 we have controls and can provide the policy and SOC 2 report.
[03:53] Mark: Good. On network firewall rules — what ports/protocols need to be open between Redwood nodes and your control plane?
[03:59] Priya: For typical deployments: outbound HTTPS (443) to the control plane endpoints if using the managed control plane; for artifact S3 we use VPC endpoints, so no internet needed. For runtime Redis/KV cache and internal services we use gRPC on specific ports (we'll share exact ports in the diagram). The broader principle: only allow narrow egress (control plane, S3 endpoints, and egress proxy).
[04:28] Ravi: We have an egress firewall that only allows certain FQDNs; can Redwood work with FQDN allow-lists?
[04:36] Liam: Yes, we publish a fixed IP range and FQDNs for the control plane; for Private deployments you can lock down to our control-plane endpoints or, as Priya said, choose fully customer-hosted control plane.
[04:47] Elena: If we host the control plane in our account, will we still get Redwood updates and support?
[04:52] Priya: Yes — we provide tooling for house-keeping and upgrades via CI pipelines you run, plus automation bits we hand off. Support remains via Redwood, we just don't host your control plane.
[05:05] Mark: Storage residency — we need all PII to remain in eu-west-1. Is partial region pinning supported?
[05:12] Priya: Yes, you can pin workloads to specific regions and Redwood nodes placed accordingly. Artifacts and logs can be restricted to region-local storage. For cross-region failover we can replicate with agreed policies, but for your regulated models we suggest no replication outside eu-west-1.
[05:29] Sophie: SOC 2 evidence: we need network diagrams, config baselines, and audit logs for the last 6 months. Can Redwood provide those artifacts for the Private setup?
[05:38] Liam: We provide SOC 2 and ISO documents and for Private deployments we provide configuration artifacts (templates, checklist) and recommend using config management (terraform) and audit exports to satisfy auditors. We can compile a package for the auditor.
[05:54] Ravi: Firewall specifics — do you support eBPF-based firewalling or are you strictly relying on cloud SG/NSG?
[06:01] Priya: Our runtime doesn't assume a single enforcement mechanism. We can work with cloud native security groups, NACLs, and customers that want host-level eBPF controls can layer that too. We provide recommended SG templates and iptables examples for on-prem nodes.
[06:18] Mark: How about bastion or jump host pattern for admin access? We want no direct SSH from internet to private nodes.
[06:25] Priya: Standard best practice: put management in a separate management VPC or use session-manager / AWS Systems Manager, or bastion via approved jumpbox with MFA. We integrate with SAML SSO and recommends no long-lived keys, use ephemeral certs.
[06:40] Elena: On SSO and RBAC — we use Okta and need SCIM provisioning for user sync. Can Redwood sync roles and enforce least privilege per team?
[06:48] Liam: Yes, Redwood supports SAML for SSO and SCIM for provisioning. RBAC is role-based and map-able to Okta groups. You can create scopes like model-deploy, model-run, audit-view, and tie those to SCIM groups.
[07:02] Sophie: Can we enforce approval workflows for model rollouts? Auditors ask for change control.
[07:07] Priya: Yes, we have canary and manual-approval rollouts; audit trail records who approved what and when. That audit trail is exportable to your SIEM.
[07:19] Mark: Performance question — if we route egress through a proxy and do TLS inspection, is there a latency impact on inference?
[07:27] Priya: Some impact is expected; we recommend colocating the egress proxy in the same AZ and tuning keep-alive and TLS session reuse. For latency-sensitive endpoints, Redwood supports a direct peered path with approved IPs to minimize proxy hop — but that depends on your compliance allowance.
[07:46] Ravi: For on-prem HSM, what protocols do you support? PKCS#11? KMIP?
[07:51] Priya: PKCS#11 and KMIP are supported; we typically integrate via PKCS#11 for local HSM modules. We'll share integration docs and example configs.
[08:02] Elena: Any guidance on logging level — we don't want to log PII but need sufficient telemetry to investigate incidents.
[08:09] Priya: Agree — default is metadata + metrics; request/response payload logging is opt-in and should be used with redaction patterns. We'll provide regex-based redaction examples and sample masking lib.
[08:21] Liam: Quick interjection — competitor question: some vendors push a managed VPC connector that opens up lots of ports. We avoid that by providing narrow, documented egress and supporting fully customer-hosted control plane.
[08:33] Mark: Good. Pen test — do you allow third-party pentests on Redwood nodes in our VPC?
[08:40] Priya: Yes, for Private deployments we allow customer-run pen tests on nodes you control. For co-located or managed nodes we have a coordinated pentest process. We can share our policy and request form.
[08:53] Sophie: For compliance reporting, is there a standard report bundle you provide?
[08:57] Liam: SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001 summary, config checklist, and a runbook for incident response. For Private deployments, we add the customer-specific config baselines.
[09:10] Ravi: Anything else we should consider for firewalling — egress DNS, DoH, blocked IP ranges?
[09:17] Priya: DNS egress is important — enforce DNS over your resolver, block direct public DNS, and consider only allowing FQDNs via egress proxy. We also recommend limiting ephemeral outbound ports and keeping NACL explicit.
[09:30] Elena: Ok can we walk through a sample network diagram now?
[09:33] Priya: Sure — (shares diagram). So here: management VPC with SSM and bastion, runtime VPC with private subnets running Redwood nodes, egress VPC with proxy appliances, TGW connecting accounts, and private endpoints for S3 and KMS. The control plane endpoints are reachable only from management subnets or via a private connection.
[09:56] Mark: How do upgrades work? We can't accept uncontrolled restarts.
[10:01] Priya: Upgrades are orchestrated; we support rolling upgrades, maintenance windows, and can stage to canaries. For high availability we recommend multi-AZ node groups and pinned capacity.
[10:12] Liam: Let's capture next steps — Priya will send the network diagram and firewall templates; Mark will share current infra diagrams; Sophie will send compliance list; we'll schedule pen-test scoping.
[10:24] Mark: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.

End of transcript (notes: audio had some overlap at ~00:40 where a couple of participants spoke; a couple of terms transcribed imperfectly such as "KV cash" instead of "KV cache" and "H S M" spacing).
